extracted.intended_audience: typesetters, printers, book designers, and typographers
extracted.subtask_description: Specimen pages showing the Monotype family in multiple point sizes and settings (solid vs leaded) to judge legibility, emphasis, and hierarchy for book printing. Useful for choosing point size, leading, and display capitalization for different textual roles (body, heading, display).

rubrics_metrics.name: Point size designation (e.g., Six Point, Seven Point, Eight Point, Nine Point, Ten Point, Eleven Point, Twelve Point, Six Point Cushing No. Twenty-Five)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specimen repeats the same passage in a range of labeled point sizes (SIX POINT NO. THIRTY-ONE, SEVEN POINT NO. THIRTY-ONE, EIGHT POINT NO. EIGHT, NINE POINT NO. THIRTY-ONE, TEN POINT NO. THIRTY-ONE, ELEVEN POINT NO. THIRTY-ONE, TWELVE POINT NO. THIRTY-ONE, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the samples to compare readability and optical weight at intended reading distances and formats; choose smaller point sizes for compact body text and larger sizes for headings or display. The specimens present the same paragraph across sizes specifically to make visual comparison straightforward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solid vs. Leaded setting
rubrics_metrics.description: Each point-size specimen is shown in two settings labeled “[Solid]” and “[Leaded]”.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare tight (solid) leading with added (leaded) leading to judge line spacing for legibility and aesthetic preference. Smaller point sizes often benefit from leaded settings to improve readability; displays or captions may use solid setting for compactness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type family identification — MONOTYPE
rubrics_metrics.description: All samples are presented under the heading “MONOTYPE” indicating the specific type foundry/family being demonstrated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Monotype specimens to judge that particular face’s characteristics (stroke weight, serifs, rhythm) across sizes and settings before selecting it for a book or printed work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of identical sample prose for comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: The same running passage (“When thoughtful Greeks like Polybius saw the fall of Carthage and of Corinth...”) is repeated in each specimen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presenting identical text allows direct visual comparison of letterforms, word color, spacing, hyphenation, and overall texture across sizes and settings; designers should use representative prose (not nonsense text) when evaluating type for body copy to reveal real-world hyphenation and word shapes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Display capitalization and emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Specimens include lines in full uppercase for emphasis/display (e.g., “MANIFEST GAIN OF A GREAT PEACE THROUGHOUT THE WORLD”, “A WORLD-EMPIRE, INCLUDING ALL THE LANDS AND NATIONS ABOUT THE MEDITERRANEAN SEA”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate uppercase lines in context to determine when ALL-CAPS is appropriate (short headings, display lines) and how it affects legibility and visual weight; avoid long runs of uppercase for body text as shown by the specimen contrast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchy and layout cues (point size + caps + leading)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specimens demonstrate how combinations of point size, leading (solid/leaded), and capitalization create a typographic hierarchy between body copy and headings/display lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the specimen combinations to establish rules for headings, subheadings, and body text in a publication — e.g., larger point size + caps for headings, standard point size + leaded setting for body copy. The page shows practical examples of these combinations for decision-making.
